overview.intro:
Chapter 08 covers fruit and nuts — fresh, chilled, frozen, dried or provisionally preserved — plus citrus and melon peel. Its **240 tariff lines** carry mostly small printed rates (11.2¢/kg on avocados, 1.1¢/kg on strawberries, Free on bananas and blueberries), but a few are steep and seasonal: cantaloupes entered outside August 1–September 15 pay 29.8%, other melons 28%, frozen strawberries 11.2%.

The U.S. imported **$25.66B** of Chapter 08 goods in 2025; Mexico alone supplied 40% and USMCA-qualifying Mexican and Canadian produce enters free. Since July 24, 2026 most other suppliers add a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%** — Peru and Chile +12.5%, Guatemala and Ecuador +10%, 10% in total for the EU — but **77 lines are exempt**: bananas, avocados, pineapples, mangoes, oranges, limes, coconuts, cashews and other tropical fruit and nuts (U.S. note 52(b)). For fresh fruit, USDA APHIS decides whether a fruit may come from a given country at all.

productGroups.label: Coconuts, Brazil nuts & cashews
productGroups.blurb: Coconuts, Brazil nuts and cashews are Free on every line and on the Section 301 exemption list, so they enter duty-free from any country except China (older Section 301 lists). Vietnam supplied $768M, mostly shelled cashews.

productGroups.label: Other nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, pistachios, pecans…)
productGroups.blurb: Most nuts pay a per-kilogram rate — shelled almonds 24¢/kg, shelled walnuts 26.5¢/kg, shelled pecans 17.6¢/kg, pistachios 0.9–1.9¢/kg — and the Section 301 duty. Chestnuts, macadamias, pine, kola and areca nuts are exempt from Section 301.

productGroups.label: Bananas & plantains
productGroups.blurb: Bananas are Free and exempt from Section 301; only dried plantains carry a duty (1.4%). Guatemala, Ecuador, Costa Rica, Colombia and Honduras ship most of the volume.

productGroups.label: Dates, figs, pineapples, avocados, guavas & mangoes
productGroups.blurb: The largest group by value. Avocados pay 11.2¢/kg (Free under USMCA), pineapples 0.44–1.1¢/kg, mangoes 6.6¢/kg fresh — all three exempt from Section 301. Dates (up to 29.8%) and figs are not exempt.

productGroups.label: Citrus fruit
productGroups.blurb: Oranges, mandarins and grapefruit pay 1.5–2.5¢/kg, limes 0.8% or 1.8¢/kg. Oranges and limes are exempt from Section 301; lemons, mandarins and grapefruit are not. Grapefruit rates change with the month of entry.

productGroups.label: Grapes & raisins
productGroups.blurb: Fresh table grapes pay $1.13 or $1.80 per cubic meter and are Free from April 1 to June 30; raisins pay 1.8–2.8¢/kg. Not exempt from Section 301 — Peru and Chile pay +12.5%.

productGroups.label: Melons, watermelons & papayas
productGroups.blurb: The highest base rates in the chapter, and seasonal: watermelons 9% (December–March) or 17%, cantaloupes 12.8% (August 1–September 15) or 29.8%, other melons 5.4% or 28%. Papayas (5.4%) are exempt from Section 301.

productGroups.label: Apples, pears & quinces
productGroups.blurb: Apples are Free; pears and quinces are Free from April 1 to June 30 and 0.3¢/kg otherwise. Quinces are exempt from Section 301.

productGroups.label: Apricots, cherries, peaches, plums
productGroups.blurb: Cherries and nectarines are Free, apricots 0.2¢/kg, plums Free January–May and 0.5¢/kg otherwise. None is exempt from Section 301 — cherries from Chile pay 12.5%.

productGroups.label: Other fresh fruit (berries, kiwifruit, tropical fruit)
productGroups.blurb: Berries are the second-largest group: blueberries, raspberries and blackberries are Free or near-free at base but pay the Section 301 duty. Kiwifruit, durians, lychee, dragon fruit and other tropical fruit are exempt.

productGroups.label: Frozen fruit & nuts
productGroups.blurb: Frozen fruit is mostly ad valorem: strawberries 11.2%, raspberries 4.5%, mangoes 10.9%, cherries and other fruit 14.5%; blueberries are Free. Frozen bananas, pineapples, mangoes, papayas and coconut meat are exempt from Section 301.

productGroups.label: Fruit provisionally preserved
productGroups.blurb: Fruit preserved only for transport (in brine, sulfur water or SO₂) and not edible as entered: cherries 13.4¢/kg, fruit mixtures 11.2%.

productGroups.label: Dried fruit (prunes, apricots…) & mixtures
productGroups.blurb: Dried apricots 1.8¢/kg, dried apples 0.74¢/kg, dried blueberries 1.4¢/kg; dried prunes and mixtures of nuts or dried fruit pay 14%. None is exempt from Section 301.

productGroups.label: Citrus & melon peel
productGroups.blurb: Orange and citron peel are Free; lime and other peel 1.6¢/kg.

workedExamples.title: 18,000 kg of Hass avocados from Michoacán
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 11.2¢/kg: 18,000 × $0.112 = **$2,016**. With a USMCA claim (SPI **S**) it is **$0**. Avocados are on the Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86), so even a Mexican shipment that does not qualify for USMCA pays only the $2,016 — no 10% on top.

workedExamples.title: $100,000 of fresh blueberries from Peru
workedExamples.body: Blueberries are Free at base, but Peru is one of the 60 Section 301 economies and blueberries are not exempt: 12.5% × $100,000 = **$12,500** (9903.05.63). Claiming the Peru TPA does not help — it removes only the base rate, which is already Free.

workedExamples.title: $60,000 of table grapes from Chile entered in March
workedExamples.body: Grapes entered February 15–March 31 are $1.13/m³, which the Chile FTA (SPI **CL**) makes Free. The Section 301 duty for Chile still applies: 12.5% × $60,000 = **$7,500** (9903.05.30). The same grapes entered April 1–June 30 would be Free at base but still pay the $7,500.

workedExamples.title: $250,000 of shelled cashews from Vietnam
workedExamples.body: Cashews are Free and on the Section 301 exemption list, so the duty is **$0** — although Vietnam pays +12.5% on most other goods (9903.05.84). Shelled walnuts from Vietnam, by contrast, pay 26.5¢/kg plus 12.5%.

**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover inedible nuts or fruit.

**Note 2.** Chilled fruit and nuts are to be classified in the same headings as the corresponding fresh fruit and nuts.

**Note 3.** Dried fruit or dried nuts of this chapter may be partially rehydrated, or treated for the following purposes: (a) for additional preservation or stabilization (for example, by moderate heat treatment, sulfuring, the addition of sorbic acid or potassium sorbate); (b) to improve or maintain their appearance (for example, by the addition of vegetable oil or small quantities of glucose syrup), provided that they retain the character of dried fruits or dried nuts.

seo.title: HTS Chapter 08 Fruit & Nuts Tariff Updates 2026 — What Changed Since January 2025 | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 08 (fruit and nuts) since January 2025: unchanged base rates, the end of the IEEPA duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on Peru, Chile, Vietnam and others, the fruit exempt from them, and USDA import rules — with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 08 base rate changed; 14 new 10-digit statistical lines split out certified-organic fruit, wild blueberries and grapefruit entered in October.

The changes came on top of the base rate. The 2025 IEEPA duties (Mexico and Canada +25% or +35% on non-USMCA goods, the reciprocal tariff of 10% or more on everyone else) **ended on February 24, 2026**; from November 13, 2025 bananas, avocados, pineapples, mangoes, oranges, limes, coconuts, cashews and other tropical produce had already been exempt from the reciprocal tariff. The 10% Section 122 surcharge that followed (with the same produce exempt) expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, fruit and nuts from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%** — Peru, Chile, Costa Rica, Colombia and Vietnam +12.5%, Guatemala, Ecuador and Honduras +10% — except on the **77 exempt lines**. Brazil pays +37.5% and China up to +37.5%. **USMCA-qualifying produce from Mexico and Canada is exempt.**

For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: Section 301 (2026, 60 economies) takes effect
changes.detail: +10% or +12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), with EU goods at 10% and Japan, South Korea and Switzerland at 12.5% in total where the base rate is lower. In Chapter 08 it reaches 163 of 240 lines; the other 77 are on the exemption list (9903.05.86) — the same tropical fruit and nuts that were exempt from the reciprocal tariff and the Section 122 surcharge. USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 (Brazil) takes effect
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01), except the subheadings on its exemption list (9903.05.03) — the same 77 Chapter 08 lines exempt from the 60-economy action. From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply to Mexican and Canadian fruit.

changes.title: Proposed: wider access for fresh pineapple from the Philippines and Thailand
changes.detail: APHIS proposed letting all varieties of fresh pineapple from the Philippines and Thailand into all U.S. ports, and Thai pineapple without irradiation. The comment period closed August 10, 2026; no final decision had been published as of October 11, 2026.

changes.title: Imported avocado maturity rules changed
changes.detail: AMS changed the South Florida avocado maturity schedule so certain sizes of the Beta variety can ship earlier, and made the matching change to the Section 8e avocado import regulation (7 CFR 944.31).

changes.title: Proposed: fresh pineapple from Taiwan to all U.S. states
changes.detail: APHIS proposed allowing any variety of fresh pineapple from Taiwan into any U.S. state or territory (today only at least 50% Smooth Cayenne, into Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands). The comment period closed May 4, 2026; no final decision had been published as of October 11, 2026.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Forty-eight Chapter 08 subheadings — bananas, avocados, pineapples, mangoes, oranges, limes, coconuts, cashews and other tropical produce — were on the product exemption lists (9903.03.03, 9903.03.04); USMCA-qualifying goods from Mexico and Canada were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Proposed: smaller minimum size for imported kiwifruit
changes.detail: AMS proposed relaxing the minimum size for kiwifruit (except Actinidia chinensis) under the California marketing order and the Section 8e kiwifruit import regulation (7 CFR 944.550). Comments closed April 7, 2026; no final rule had been published as of October 11, 2026.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 renewed AGOA (SPI D) retroactively from September 30, 2025. Most dutiable Chapter 08 lines list D in the Special column. GSP (SPI A, A+, A*) remains expired since December 31, 2020, so GSP claims pay the general rate.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 duty on products of Nicaragua rises to 10% (2027) and 15% (2028)
changes.detail: USTR set a Section 301 duty, phased in over two years, on products of Nicaragua entered at the general rate (9903.89.01): +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. Goods originating under CAFTA-DR are not covered (U.S. note 29(a)). Where it applies it reaches every Chapter 08 line, including the fruit exempt from the 2026 action, and stacks with the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty on Nicaragua (9903.05.58) on non-exempt lines.

changes.title: Tropical fruit and nuts exempted from the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14360 added agricultural products to the reciprocal-tariff exemption list (U.S. note 2(v)(iii) to Chapter 99), including 48 Chapter 08 subheadings: bananas, plantains, avocados, pineapples, mangoes, guavas, oranges, limes, papayas, kiwifruit, coconuts, cashews, Brazil nuts, macadamias and other tropical produce. Executive Order 14361 made a similar change to Brazil's 40% IEEPA duty from the same date. Grapes, berries, apples, lemons, almonds and most other temperate fruit and nuts stayed covered until the IEEPA duties ended.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: Walnut import regulation stayed
changes.detail: AMS stayed the Section 8e grade and size regulation for imported walnuts (7 CFR 999.100) to match the suspended California walnut handling rules, so imported walnuts no longer need USDA grade inspection.

changes.title: Additional 40% IEEPA duty on products of Brazil
changes.detail: +40% on Brazilian goods (Executive Order 14323, signed July 30, 2025), with an annex of exempt products; narrowed for agricultural products from November 13, 2025 (Executive Order 14361). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: New Zealand fruit no longer needs a light brown apple moth declaration
changes.detail: APHIS removed the requirement that fruit from New Zealand (including kiwifruit and apples) carry a phytosanitary-certificate declaration of freedom from light brown apple moth.

changes.title: Fresh pineapple from Indonesia authorized
changes.detail: APHIS authorized fresh pineapple fruit for consumption from Indonesia under designated phytosanitary measures.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Section 8e import inspection fees charged per pound
changes.detail: AMS moved Section 8e import inspection fees (avocados, citrus, grapes, kiwifruit, dates, nuts, raisins and other 8e commodities) from a per-carlot to a per-pound basis, with half-price additional sublots. The rule was published December 30, 2024 and its effective date delayed to March 20, 2025.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), raised to +35% from August 1, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of fruit and nuts were **$25.66B in 2025**, 1.4% less than in 2024 ($26.02B) and 32% more than in 2020 ($19.47B). **Mexico** supplied $10.36B (40%) — avocados and other 0804 fruit ($3.98B) and berries ($3.40B) — and fell 6.5%, while **Peru** grew 16.8% to $3.48B on table grapes and blueberries. Chile ($2.51B), Guatemala ($1.83B) and Costa Rica ($1.37B) follow.

By product, **avocados** (0804.40, $3.80B), **bananas** (0803.90, $2.89B) and **fresh grapes** (0806.10, $2.83B) lead, then blueberries and cranberries (0810.40, $2.29B) and raspberries and blackberries (0810.20, $1.69B). Shelled cashews, mostly from Vietnam, fell 20% to $858M.

The duty actually paid is small relative to the value. Mexico and Canada ship mostly under USMCA, the Central and South American suppliers claim CAFTA-DR, Chile, Peru or Colombia FTA rates, and subheadings worth about $11.8B in 2025 — avocados, bananas, pineapples, mangoes, oranges, cashews, kiwifruit and other tropical produce — are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty. Peru, Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia still pay +12.5% (Guatemala, Ecuador and Honduras +10%) on non-exempt fruit such as grapes, blueberries, cherries and melons since July 24, 2026. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so none of these figures yet reflect that duty.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on fruit and nuts depends on **where it comes from and whether the fruit is on the exemption list**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule.

**USMCA-qualifying produce from Mexico and Canada enters free.** Peru, Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia claim FTA rates that zero the base rate but still pay the **12.5% Section 301 duty** on grapes, berries, cherries and other non-exempt fruit; Guatemala, Ecuador and Honduras pay 10%. **Bananas, avocados, pineapples, mangoes, limes, oranges and cashews are exempt**, so for the largest tropical lanes the total is still Free.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 08: Edible Fruit and Nuts — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Fruit & Nuts: APHIS Permits, Phytosanitary Rules & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 08) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The permits, certificates and inspections for each HTS Chapter 08 line — USDA APHIS fruit rules and treatments, USDA AMS Section 8e grade inspection, FDA prior notice and FSVP — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTAs, seasonal rates and the Section 301 exemption list.
keywords: import fruit into the us requirements

tariffEngineering.intro:
For fresh fruit the first question is not the rate but **whether the fruit may come from that country at all**: USDA APHIS lists every approved fruit-and-origin pair, often with a treatment (cold, heat or irradiation) or a pest-free area. Avocados, citrus, grapes, kiwifruit, dates and several nuts must also pass **USDA AMS Section 8e** grade inspection, and all food needs FDA prior notice and a Foreign Supplier Verification Program.

The ways to pay less are written into the schedule: claim **USMCA** for Mexican and Canadian produce, an **FTA rate** for Chile, Peru, Colombia or CAFTA-DR fruit, **time the entry** for seasonal lines, and report the **Section 301 exemption** for tropical fruit and nuts. Each depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Claim USMCA on fruit and nuts from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty on goods of Mexico or Canada, plus the base rate (for example 11.2¢/kg on avocados, up to 29.8% on out-of-season cantaloupes)
levers.appliesTo: All 240 lines, for goods that originate under USMCA (fruit grown in Mexico or Canada is wholly obtained)
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer. It need not follow a set form; it can be on the invoice or another document, and CBP can ask for it.
levers.caveat: Without a valid claim, a Mexican or Canadian shipment pays the base rate plus 10% on the 163 lines that are not on the Section 301 exemption list. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim the free trade agreement rate (Chile, Peru, CAFTA-DR, Colombia and others)
levers.saves: The base rate: almost every dutiable Chapter 08 line is Free under the FTAs listed in its Special column (for example 24¢/kg on shelled almonds, 1.1¢/kg on strawberries, 11.2% on frozen strawberries)
levers.appliesTo: Lines whose Special column lists the partner (CL, PE, P, CO, AU, KR, IL, MA, PA and others)
levers.document: The FTA claim on the entry (SPI code) backed by the origin information the agreement requires.
levers.caveat: An FTA claim removes the base rate only. The 2026 Section 301 duty still applies to FTA goods (U.S. note 52(a) to Chapter 99 subchapter III): Chile, Peru, Colombia, Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic pay +12.5%, Guatemala and Honduras +10%, unless the line is on the exemption list.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Time the entry: many fruit rates change with the calendar
levers.saves: The difference between the in-season and out-of-season rate, set by the date of entry: table grapes Free from April 1 to June 30 (else $1.13 or $1.80 per m³); pears and quinces Free April 1–June 30 (else 0.3¢/kg); plums Free January 1–May 31 (else 0.5¢/kg); watermelons 9% December 1–March 31 (else 17%); cantaloupes 12.8% August 1–September 15 (else 29.8%); other melons 5.4% December 1–May 31 (else 28%); strawberries 0.2¢/kg June 15–September 15 (else 1.1¢/kg)
levers.appliesTo: Lines split by entry period in headings 0804, 0805, 0806, 0807, 0808, 0809 and 0810
levers.document: None beyond the entry: the rate in force on the date of entry (or withdrawal from warehouse) applies.
levers.caveat: Perishable fruit rarely waits for a cheaper season; the split matters most for melons, where the gap is up to 17 points. The Section 301 duty does not change with the season.

levers.title: Declare the Section 301 exemption for listed fruit and nuts
levers.saves: The whole 2026 Section 301 duty (+10% or +12.5%, and 10% or 12.5% in place of the base rate for the EU, Japan and others) on the 77 exempt lines; for Brazil also the 25% Brazil Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: Coconuts, Brazil nuts, cashews, chestnuts, macadamias, kola, areca and pine nuts, bananas and plantains, pineapples, avocados, mangoes and guavas, oranges, limes, papayas, quinces, kiwifruit, durians, tamarinds and other berries of 0810.90.27, lychee, dragon fruit and other 0810.90.46 fruit, several frozen tropical fruits and provisionally preserved pineapple (U.S. note 52(b)); etrogs (0805.90.01) and frozen tropical fruit nesoi (0811.90.80) on declaration (note 52(c))
levers.document: Report heading 9903.05.86 (listed subheadings) or 9903.05.87 (etrogs, frozen tropical fruit nesoi) with the Chapter 08 line; for 9903.05.87 the goods must match the description.
levers.caveat: Lemons, grapes, berries other than those listed, apples, cherries, almonds, walnuts, pistachios, dates, figs and dried fruit are not exempt. China still pays its older Section 301 List 3 or 4A duty on exempt lines.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(b)–(c)

levers.title: Send 8e-regulated fruit to processing under an SC-6 certificate
levers.saves: The Section 8e grade, size and quality inspection (and its fee) for avocados, grapefruit, oranges, table grapes, kiwifruit, fresh prunes, dates, hazelnuts, pistachios, raisins and dried prunes going to processing, animal feed or charity
levers.appliesTo: Fruit and nuts covered by 7 CFR part 944 and part 999
levers.document: An Importers Exempt Commodity Form (SC-6 certificate), filed electronically through AMS’s Compliance and Enforcement Management System (CEMS), ideally before the shipment arrives.
levers.caveat: This saves inspection, not duty. Pistachios still need the aflatoxin certificate, and APHIS and FDA rules still apply.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty: a ruling fixes the line (fresh vs dried vs provisionally preserved, mixtures, frozen) before the goods arrive, and with it the base rate and whether the Section 301 exemption applies
levers.appliesTo: Any line where classification decides the rate, for example 0811 vs 0812 vs Chapter 20, or nut mixtures in 0813.50
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product and how it is processed and packed.
levers.caveat: A ruling applies to the transaction described; a different product or process may need its own.

rules.title: Fresh fruit: APHIS import permit, fruit and origin listed in ACIR, port inspection; most origins also need a phytosanitary certificate and some need treatment or a systems approach

citations.label: APHIS ACIR database (approved fruit by country)

rules.title: Fruit fly and other pest treatments: cold treatment, heat (vapor or hot water) or irradiation where ACIR requires it, under the PPQ Treatment Manual
Pest-free areas: some fruit may come only from an area APHIS recognizes as free of a pest (for example fruit flies)
Fruit grown in Canada: no APHIS permit needed, but still subject to inspection
Dried, cured or processed fruit and nuts (including raisins, cured figs and dates, nuts): no APHIS permit, except certain chestnuts and acorns
Frozen fruit: imported under the general fruit rules and held under the frozen-product requirements of 7 CFR part 305
Avocados: Section 8e grade and maturity requirements and AMS inspection (maturity schedule changed April 8, 2026)
Grapefruit and oranges: Section 8e grade, size and maturity requirements and AMS inspection
Table grapes: Section 8e grade and size requirements and AMS inspection
Raisins: Section 8e grade requirements and inspection
Kiwifruit: Section 8e grade, size and maturity requirements and AMS inspection (size change proposed February 6, 2026)
Fresh prune-variety plums and dried prunes: Section 8e grade and size requirements and inspection
Dates (other than for processing): Section 8e grade requirements and inspection
Hazelnuts: Section 8e grade and size requirements; pistachios: aflatoxin certificate from a USDA or USDA-accredited laboratory for each lot; walnut import regulation stayed since November 6, 2025

Section 8e: imports of covered fruit and nuts must meet the grade, size, quality and maturity rules of the matching domestic marketing order while it is regulating; inspection fees charged per pound since March 20, 2025
All food: prior notice before arrival, registered foreign facility (packing houses, processors), and a Foreign Supplier Verification Program kept by the U.S. importer
Fresh produce: the foreign farm must meet the Produce Safety Rule (the importer verifies this under FSVP)
Food Traceability List items (for example fresh melons, tropical tree fruits, fresh-cut fruit): key-event records; FDA will not enforce before July 20, 2028
Certified organic lines: an NOP Import Certificate for each organic shipment

groups.label: Coconuts, Brazil nuts & cashews
groups.note: Dried coconut and shelled or in-shell nuts need no APHIS permit; fresh coconuts are fresh fruit under 7 CFR 319.56 (APHIS published a risk analysis for fresh coconuts from Belize on September 17, 2026). Every line here is Free and on the Section 301 exemption list.

groups.label: Other nuts (almonds, hazelnuts, walnuts, pistachios, pecans…)
groups.note: Nuts are dried products for APHIS (chestnuts are the exception), but hazelnuts and pistachios meet Section 8e rules, and pistachios need an aflatoxin certificate per lot.

groups.label: Bananas & plantains
groups.note: Fresh bananas and plantains enter under APHIS fruit rules; bananas are Free and exempt from the Section 301 duty.

groups.label: Dates, figs, pineapples, avocados, guavas & mangoes
groups.note: Avocados need an APHIS-approved origin listed in ACIR and meet Section 8e grade and maturity rules; mangoes from many origins need a hot-water or irradiation treatment. Dates and dried figs are dried products for APHIS; dates also meet Section 8e rules.

groups.label: Citrus fruit
groups.note: Grapefruit and oranges meet Section 8e rules. Citrus from many origins needs a fruit fly treatment or pest-free area; lemons and limes are not 8e commodities.

groups.label: Grapes & raisins
groups.note: Fresh table grapes meet Section 8e rules and, from some origins, cold treatment or fumigation; raisins are a dried product for APHIS but meet Section 8e grade rules.

groups.label: Melons, watermelons & papayas
groups.note: Melons are on the FDA Food Traceability List. Rates depend on the entry date (watermelons 9% or 17%, cantaloupes 12.8% or 29.8%).

groups.label: Apricots, cherries, peaches, plums
groups.note: Fresh prune-variety plums meet Section 8e rules; cherries and stone fruit from some origins need cold treatment or a systems approach.

groups.label: Other fresh fruit (berries, kiwifruit, tropical fruit)
groups.note: Kiwifruit meets Section 8e rules. Berries, lychee, rambutan and dragon fruit often need a treatment (irradiation or cold) depending on origin; tropical tree fruits are on the FDA Food Traceability List.

groups.label: Frozen fruit & nuts
groups.note: Frozen fruit enters under 7 CFR 319.56-12; frozen tropical fruit nesoi (0811.90.80) can claim the Section 301 exemption under 9903.05.87.

groups.label: Fruit provisionally preserved
groups.note: Fruit provisionally preserved (for example cherries in brine) and unsuitable for eating as entered.

groups.label: Dried fruit (prunes, apricots…) & mixtures
groups.note: Dried prunes meet Section 8e rules; dried apricots, apples, berries and mixtures need FDA entry only.

groups.label: Citrus & melon peel
groups.note: Dried or brined citrus peel is a processed product; fresh peel follows the fresh-fruit rules.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations — not legal advice. Fruit import approvals and treatments differ by country and change often; check the APHIS ACIR database and your permit before each shipment.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on fruit and nuts — by country and product, HS codes and entry rules. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: USMCA-qualifying fruit and nuts from Mexico and Canada enter free — no base rate, no extra duty.

The 2025 IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026. Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5% applies to fruit from 60 economies, including Peru, Chile, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Colombia, Ecuador and Vietnam — but 77 lines (bananas, avocados, pineapples, mangoes, oranges, limes, cashews, coconuts and other tropical produce) are exempt.
For fresh fruit, USDA APHIS approval of the fruit and origin decides whether it can enter at all; avocados, citrus, grapes, kiwifruit, dates and some nuts also need USDA grade inspection.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on avocados from Mexico?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on avocados from mexico
are there tariffs on mexican avocados
faqs.answer: Not if they qualify for USMCA: avocados (0804.40) have a base rate of 11.2¢/kg that USMCA makes Free, and avocados are on the Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86). A Mexican shipment that does not qualify pays only the 11.2¢/kg — about $2,016 on an 18,000 kg load — with no 10% on top. The 25% IEEPA duty of 2025 never applied to USMCA goods and ended on February 24, 2026. The U.S. imported $3.80B of avocados in 2025, most of it from Mexico.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on bananas?
searchedAs: did trump put tariffs on bananas
faqs.answer: No. Fresh bananas (0803.90) are Free at base, and bananas were taken off the reciprocal tariff from November 13, 2025 (Executive Order 14360). They are on the Section 301 exemption list (9903.05.86), so bananas from Guatemala, Ecuador, Costa Rica, Colombia or Honduras pay no Section 301 duty either. Only dried plantains carry a base rate (1.4%). China is the exception: its older Section 301 lists still apply.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on blueberries from Peru?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on blueberries from peru
is there a tariff on blueberries
faqs.answer: Yes, since July 24, 2026: 12.5% of value under the Section 301 duty on goods of Peru (9903.05.63). Fresh blueberries (0810.40) are Free at base, so the Peru TPA does not lower the bill, and blueberries are not on the exemption list. Blueberries from Mexico that qualify for USMCA remain duty-free; from Chile they also pay 12.5%.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on fruits and vegetables from Mexico?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on fruits and vegetables from mexico
are there tariffs on fruit from mexico
is there tariffs on fruits and vegetables
mexico tariff on edible fruit and nuts
faqs.answer: For fruit that qualifies for USMCA, no — the base rate is Free and the 10% Section 301 duty on Mexican goods does not apply (9903.05.94). Mexico supplied $10.36B of the $25.66B of fruit and nuts imported in 2025. Mexican fruit that does not qualify pays the base rate plus 10% on non-exempt lines such as berries, lemons and melons; avocados, limes and mangoes pay only the base rate. Vegetables are in Chapter 07.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on cashews?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on cashews
faqs.answer: Cashews (0801.31 in shell, 0801.32 shelled) are Free and on the Section 301 exemption list, so cashews from Vietnam, India or Africa enter duty-free even though Vietnam pays +12.5% on most other goods. Only Chinese cashews pay a Section 301 duty (the older List 3 or 4A rate). The U.S. imported $858M of shelled cashews in 2025.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on mangoes?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on mangoes
faqs.answer: Fresh mangoes (0804.50) pay 6.6¢/kg, which USMCA, the Peru, Colombia and Chile agreements and CAFTA-DR make Free. Mangoes are exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, so the base rate is the whole tariff. Most origins must treat mangoes (hot water or irradiation) under APHIS rules.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on grapes?
faqs.answer: Fresh table grapes (0806.10) are $1.13 per cubic meter from February 15 to March 31, Free from April 1 to June 30 and $1.80 per cubic meter otherwise; the Chile and Peru agreements make all of these Free. Grapes are not exempt from Section 301, so Chilean and Peruvian grapes pay 12.5% of value since July 24, 2026 — $7,500 on a $60,000 load. Imported table grapes must also meet USDA Section 8e grade rules.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on nuts?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on nuts
faqs.answer: It depends on the nut. Cashews, Brazil nuts, coconuts, chestnuts, macadamias and pine nuts are Free or nearly so and exempt from Section 301. Almonds (24¢/kg shelled), walnuts (26.5¢/kg shelled), hazelnuts, pecans and pistachios (0.9–1.9¢/kg) pay a per-kilogram rate plus the Section 301 duty for the country — for example 12.5% for Turkey or Vietnam. Imported pistachios also need an aflatoxin certificate for each lot (7 CFR 999.600).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for avocados?
faqs.answer: Fresh or dried avocados are 0804.40; the U.S. 10-digit lines are 0804.40.00.20 (Hass and Hass-like, certified organic), 0804.40.00.40 (other Hass) and 0804.40.00.90 (other avocados), all at 11.2¢/kg. Frozen avocado goes to 0811.90.80 (14.5%), and avocado oil is in Chapter 15, not here.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for bananas?
faqs.answer: Bananas other than plantains are 0803.90 (Free), split into certified organic, other fresh and dried. Plantains are 0803.10 — fresh Free, dried 1.4%. Frozen bananas are 0811.90.10 (3.4%); banana chips and other prepared bananas are in Chapter 20.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for cashew nuts?
searchedAs: hs code for raw cashew nuts
faqs.answer: Raw cashews in shell are 0801.31 and shelled cashew kernels 0801.32, both Free. Roasted or salted cashews are prepared nuts, classified in Chapter 20 (2008.19), not Chapter 08.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for dates?
faqs.answer: Dates are 0804.10: whole dates packed in units of 4.6 kg or less are 0804.10.20 (13.2¢/kg), larger packs with pits 0804.10.40 (1¢/kg) or pitted 0804.10.60 (2.8¢/kg), and other dates (for example chopped) 0804.10.80 at 29.8%. Dates are not exempt from Section 301, and dates for direct sale must meet USDA Section 8e grade rules.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for dried fruits and nuts?
searchedAs: hs code for dried fruits and nuts
hs code for mix dry fruit
faqs.answer: Dried fruit is in Chapter 08 by fruit: raisins 0806.20, dried dates, figs, pineapples and mangoes in 0804, and other dried fruit in 0813 — apricots 0813.10 (1.8¢/kg), prunes 0813.20, apples 0813.30. Mixtures of nuts or dried fruit are 0813.50 at 14%. Dried fruit may be partially rehydrated or sulfured and stay in Chapter 08 (Chapter note 3).

faqs.question: Can I bring fruit into the U.S.?
searchedAs: bringing fruit into the us from canada
bringing dried fruit into the us
why can't you bring fruit into the us
faqs.answer: Fresh fruit must be on APHIS's approved list for its country of origin and is inspected at entry; much of it needs a permit, a phytosanitary certificate or a treatment against fruit flies and other pests (7 CFR 319.56). Fruit grown in Canada needs no APHIS permit but is still inspected, and dried, cured or processed fruit and nuts are generally exempt from the permit. Commercial shipments also need FDA prior notice and an importer with a Foreign Supplier Verification Program.

faqs.question: How much fruit does the U.S. import, and from where?
faqs.answer: $25.66B of fruit and nuts in 2025. Mexico supplied 40% ($10.36B), then Peru ($3.48B), Chile ($2.51B), Guatemala ($1.83B) and Costa Rica ($1.37B). Avocados ($3.80B), bananas ($2.89B) and fresh grapes ($2.83B) were the largest products.
